strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated problem setting—reasoning-enhanced VLM editing—where human-provided chains of factual statements, rather than just corrected labels, guide model correction, addressing a clear gap in prior VLM/LLM editing literature.

Proposes two new, conceptually interesting generality metrics (rationale generality and chain-of-error generality) that go beyond standard reliability/locality/T-Gen/I-Gen metrics and better capture whether an editor exploits the structure of the provided reasoning.

The topology-aware multimodal embedding method is a principled contribution: framing embedding evaluation via network modularity (vision/language/bimodal) gives a quantitative, theoretically grounded alternative to the largely ad hoc layer/token selection used in prior retrieval-based editors (GRACE, BalancEdit), and the paper provides supporting derivations (scale invariance, sample-size effects) in the appendix.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 4 VLMs (LLaVA-1.5-7B, InstructBLIP-7B, Qwen3-VL-4B/8B) and 2 rationale-based VQA datasets (FVQA, A-OKVQA), with 5 competitive baselines (including COT-augmented variants), sequential editing experiments up to thousands of edits, and multiple ablations (K, retrieval threshold p, key merging, embedding layer/pooling choice, weighting w).
Good attention to computational efficiency: reports per-edit wall-clock time and memory overhead from key merging, showing the method is competitive with non-COT baselines despite added capability.

Reasonably thorough reproducibility documentation in appendices (dataset construction procedures, algorithmic details for codebook update/merging, image-generation quality control, implementation hyperparameters).
weaknesses: The 'human reasoning' used for edits is drawn from pre-existing dataset rationales (FVQA/A-OKVQA) rather than elicited interactively from real users correcting the specific errors that the four evaluated VLMs actually made; this weakens the paper's central framing/motivation of realistic human-in-the-loop feedback and is never validated with an actual user study.

The evaluation pipelines for the new R-Gen and CoE-Gen metrics are themselves synthetically constructed using GPT-4o for QA/scenario generation and diffusion models for images, with correctness/quality verified by VLMs (including the very model family being edited); this raises a circularity/self-validation concern that could bias results in favor of retrieval-style approaches that directly cache these facts, and is not addressed with any human verification of the generated evaluation data.

The method introduces numerous hyperparameters and design choices (retrieval K, percentile threshold p, embedding layer selection, pooling type, weighting w, Monte Carlo sample size B and batch size n) each requiring per-VLM tuning via small-scale pre-editing experiments; while ablations are provided, this adds practical complexity and may hinder straightforward reproducibility/deployment in new settings.

Table 1 and most main-text results report point estimates without variance/significance information, despite the method's several stochastic components (Monte Carlo modularity estimation, sampled augmentations), making it hard to assess how robust the reported state-of-the-art margins are.

No explicit Limitations section; the paper only briefly gestures at future work in the conclusion (e.g., modeling errors in model-generated CoT, causal relationships among reasoning facts) without a candid discussion of failure modes, scalability limits of the growing codebook under very long edit streams, or dependency on well-formed, decomposable human rationales.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is only partially addressed: prior editors are given the same reasoning-augmented inputs ('editor-COT') but were not originally designed to exploit fine-grained rationale structure, so it is unclear whether the reported gaps reflect a fundamental advantage of ReasonEdit's design versus simply a mismatch between baseline architectures and the new task setup.

Figures 5-7 (and supplementary Figure 13) are visually dense with many small subplots, making some of the more technical topology/modularity results difficult to parse without close appendix cross-referencing, reducing the self-containedness of the main text.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and practical problem setting: editing VLMs using human-provided chain-of-reasoning feedback rather than simple label corrections, which is well motivated by realistic use cases (e.g., clinician feedback).

Proposes two new evaluation metrics (rationale generality, chain-of-error generality) with carefully constructed evaluation pipelines (multi-step QA synthesis, image generation, VQA-based quality filtering) that probe generalization beyond standard accuracy/locality metrics.

The topology-balanced dual embedding, motivated by a network-science modularity analysis of vision vs. language bias in multimodal embeddings, is a creative and principled way to choose/construct retrieval keys, and the analysis (Figs. 6-7) gives genuine insight into cross-modal embedding structure across four VLMs.

Extensive empirical evaluation: four VLMs, two datasets, five adapted baseline editors (plus reasoning-augmented 'COT' variants of each), both static and sequential (continual) editing settings, and thorough ablations (key merging, number of neighbors K, retrieval threshold, embedding layer selection).

Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed algorithmic description (Algorithm 1), extensive appendix covering dataset construction, implementation details, and hyperparameter choices; the retrieval-based design avoids weight updates and is shown to be computationally efficient relative to COT-augmented weight-editing baselines.
weaknesses: The 'human reasoning' framing is only partially grounded in actual human annotations — FVQA's supporting facts and GPT-4o-generated scenarios/questions used throughout dataset construction (Appendix B) blur the line between genuine human rationale and LLM-synthesized text, which weakens the central claim that the method is specifically leveraging 'human reasoning' as opposed to any auxiliary textual context.

The new R-Gen and CoE-Gen metrics/evaluation datasets are designed and generated by the authors specifically to probe exactly the kind of generalization ReasonEdit is engineered to produce (retrieving fact-aligned sentences for semantically similar queries), raising a risk of circularity; no external or human validation of these synthetic benchmarks is provided, and no independent/held-out task is used to corroborate the generality claims.

No real user study or genuine human-in-the-loop evaluation is conducted despite the paper's core motivation (e.g., the clinician-feedback scenario in Fig. 1); all 'human reasoning' used in experiments comes from existing dataset annotations or LLM-prompted construction, which limits the ecological validity of the central claim.

The method has many interacting components (visual evidence patchification via multi-scale cropping and VLM scoring, topology-balanced dual embedding selection via Monte Carlo modularity estimation, key-merging with a learned local radius, KNN retrieval with a percentile-based rejection threshold), each requiring several additional hyperparameters; the per-edit overhead of running patchification (multiple VLM forward passes per reasoning sentence) is not clearly quantified relative to simpler retrieval baselines like GRACE/IKE, raising practical scalability concerns.

The ablation showing network modularity is useful for selecting embedding layers/weights does not compare against a simpler and cheaper baseline (e.g., selecting the layer/weight by small-scale validation accuracy directly), so it is unclear whether the elaborate network-science machinery is necessary versus a more direct selection criterion.

Baseline comparisons rely on the authors' own 'editor-COT' adaptations of prior editors (FT-COT, MEND-COT, GRACE-COT, BalancEdit-COT), which may not be optimally tuned for reasoning-heavy inputs, potentially inflating the apparent margin over baselines.

Results in Table 1 and Figure 4 appear to be single-run point estimates without reported variance/significance testing across seeds, despite the method and baselines involving stochastic elements (sampling, Monte Carlo modularity estimation, LLM-based data generation).

The main text's limitations discussion is minimal, confined to a brief forward-looking remark in the conclusion rather than a substantive discussion of failure modes, sensitivity to noisy or adversarial human reasoning, or the cost/complexity trade-offs of the proposed pipeline.

strengths: Introduces a novel and practical problem setting: reasoning-enhanced VLM editing, where users supply chain-of-thought style corrective reasoning rather than just a corrected label, which is a meaningful generalization of prior editing setups that only correct labels.

Proposes two new, well-motivated evaluation metrics (rationale generality and chain-of-error generality) with carefully constructed evaluation datasets (including multi-step dataset synthesis and image generation with quality verification), extending the standard reliability/locality/generality suite in a way that is specific and useful to reasoning-heavy editing.

The topology-aware multimodal embedding method is a genuinely novel methodological contribution: it reframes embedding selection as a network-modularity problem borrowed from network science, with formal definitions (vision/language/bimodal modularity, unimodal bias) and proofs of scale invariance, giving a principled alternative to the ad hoc single-layer embedding choices used by prior retrieval-based editors (GRACE, BalancEdit).

Extensive empirical evaluation: four VLMs with diverse architectures and sizes, two rationale-VQA datasets, five strong baseline editors each evaluated both in original and reasoning-augmented (COT) form, plus static and sequential (continual) editing regimes with timing/efficiency comparisons.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the effects of embedding method, number of retrieved neighbors K, retrieval rejection threshold, and key-merging memory savings, which support the design choices rather than treating them as fixed hyperparameters.

Strong and consistent empirical results: ReasonEdit achieves state-of-the-art performance across nearly all metrics and models, with especially large improvements in the new rationale/chain-of-error generality metrics where baselines show minimal gains even when reasoning-augmented.
Good reproducibility practices: detailed implementation/hyperparameter descriptions, dataset construction procedures, and a stated commitment to release code and data.
weaknesses: The rationale/CoE generality evaluation datasets are synthetically constructed via GPT-4o-generated questions and diffusion-model-generated images, with only partial automatic quality verification (VQA-based check); potential noise or semantic drift in this synthetic data could affect the validity of the central new metrics.

The method's practicality depends on humans providing structured, decomposed chains of reasoning statements; the paper does not deeply discuss how robust the system is to noisy, incomplete, or poorly decomposed human reasoning, despite this being central to the motivating use case (e.g., the clinician example in Fig. 1).

The overall pipeline is fairly complex (dual embedding construction, modularity-driven layer/weighting selection, key-merging radius estimation, retrieval rejection percentile), and the paper notes that the optimal embedding layer/weight must be tuned per VLM via small-scale pre-editing experiments, which somewhat undercuts the plug-and-play appeal relative to simpler single-layer retrieval editors.

Recent specialized VLM editors (MSCKE, LiveEdit) are excluded from comparison due to implementation/pretraining requirements, leaving open how ReasonEdit compares against the most recent targeted VLM editing methods.

Scalability of the codebook/key-merging approach is only demonstrated up to a few thousand sequential edits; long-horizon behavior (e.g., tens of thousands of edits over extended deployment) is not explored.

The ablation isolates the dual embedding against single-layer embeddings but does not compare against other simpler mitigations for modality bias (e.g., naive feature normalization or late fusion), making it harder to assess how much of the gain is attributable specifically to the modularity-based network-science framing versus simpler fixes.

The impact statement is minimal/boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential risks of the human-reasoning-based editing paradigm (e.g., misuse for injecting biased or incorrect 'corrections' at scale).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem formulation: incorporating human reasoning chains into VLM editing is a meaningful extension beyond simple label-correction editors, with two new evaluation metrics (rationale generality and chain-of-error generality) that meaningfully probe generalization beyond standard image/text generality.

The topology-aware multimodal embedding contribution is conceptually interesting and reasonably well-grounded: framing embedding evaluation via network modularity gives a principled, quantitative criterion for layer/pooling/weighting selection instead of the post-hoc ablation approaches used in prior work, and the analysis (vision/language bias, modularity trade-off curves) provides genuine insight into VLM embedding structure.

Extensive empirical evaluation: four VLMs, two datasets, five baselines (plus COT-augmented variants), static and sequential editing settings, noise-robustness experiments, and multiple ablations (embedding choice, K, retrieval threshold, key merging, layer-selection criterion) demonstrate consistent, sizable improvements over baselines.
Reasonable attention to reproducibility and implementation detail, with an extensive appendix describing algorithms, hyperparameters, and dataset/metric construction procedures.
The method is computationally efficient relative to COT-augmented weight-updating baselines and appears stable across a large number of sequential edits, supporting the claimed practicality.
weaknesses: Much of the evaluation infrastructure (R-Gen questions, CoE-Gen scenarios, text rephrasings, and generated images for I-Gen/R-Gen/CoE-Gen) is synthesized by GPT-4o and diffusion models rather than derived from real human-provided feedback or naturally occurring data, which risks circularity/bias in the benchmark itself and makes it unclear whether reported gains reflect genuine reasoning-based generalization versus artifacts of the LLM/diffusion generation pipeline used to build both training signal and test sets.

The paper motivates the work with real-time human-in-the-loop feedback (e.g., a clinician cropping images and writing reasoning, Fig. 1), but the experiments actually reuse existing dataset rationales (A-OKVQA/FVQA) and automatically-generated visual evidence patches rather than collecting or simulating genuinely interactive human feedback, which somewhat overstates the practical human-reasoning-in-the-loop framing relative to what is actually tested.

Accuracy of the unedited baseline is 0.00 by construction (edit sets are defined as VLM errors), so large reported Acc gains for any editor are close to guaranteed; more informative headline comparisons (e.g., relative gains isolating ReasonEdit's added value over strong retrieval baselines like IKE/GRACE, which are already fairly close to ReasonEdit on Acc/Loc in Table 1) would clarify the actual marginal contribution.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting (error bars, multiple seeds) is provided for the main results in Table 1, despite the large number of closely-spaced comparisons between methods, making it hard to assess robustness of the state-of-the-art claims.

The method has many interacting design choices and hyperparameters (dual-embedding layer/weight selection, Monte Carlo sample size, merge thresholds, K, retrieval percentile, patch selection heuristics), increasing complexity and practical reproduction burden despite the appendix; sensitivity of end-to-end performance to compounding errors across these components (e.g., imperfect automatic visual-evidence patchification) is not deeply analyzed.

Evaluation is confined to VQA-style benchmarks (A-OKVQA, FVQA) with multiple-choice answer selection: despite the introduction's framing around high-stakes reasoning domains (e.g., dermatology), no experiments in more realistic, open-ended, or higher-stakes reasoning settings are included, leaving generalizability of the claims to such domains untested.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and underexplored problem: incorporating human-provided chain-of-thought reasoning into VLM editing, which is a natural and practical extension beyond simple label-correction editing.

The topology-balanced dual embedding method is a genuinely novel and principled idea — framing embedding selection as a graph/network-science problem (modularity, vision/language bias) is a creative way to replace the typically ad hoc choice of which VLM layer to use as retrieval keys.

Extensive experimentation across 4 VLMs (LLaVA, InstructBLIP, two Qwen3-VL sizes) and 2 datasets (FVQA, A-OKVQA), with both static and sequential editing settings, computational-efficiency comparisons, and a reasonably thorough ablation suite (K, retrieval threshold, key merging, layer/weight selection criteria).

Introduction of new evaluation axes (rationale generality, chain-of-error generality) that attempt to formalize what 'reasoning-induced generalization' should mean, going beyond standard reliability/locality/generality metrics.
Inclusion of a noisy-reasoning robustness study, which is a reasonable nod toward real-world imperfect user feedback.
weaknesses: Strong concern about evaluation circularity: ReasonEdit's codebook directly stores the exact human reasoning sentences as retrievable values, and the R-Gen/CoE-Gen metrics specifically test whether the model can reproduce answers tied to those same sentences. Because the method is essentially designed to retrieve and prepend the exact facts that the evaluation then asks about, the reported superiority on these self-introduced metrics is at least partly a function of task design rather than a demonstration of emergent 'reasoning-level generalization.'

No real human-in-the-loop evaluation despite the paper's central motivating narrative (Fig. 1, clinician feedback) being about live human interaction and reasoning elicitation. All 'human reasoning' used in experiments is repurposed from existing rationale-VQA dataset annotations (A-OKVQA, FVQA), not collected from users correcting live VLM errors, which weakens the claim that the method reflects a 'practical' editing setup.

Heavy reliance on LLM/diffusion-generated synthetic evaluation data (GPT-4o for rephrased questions/R-Gen QA synthesis, Stable Diffusion/FLUX for I-Gen, R-Gen, and CoE-Gen images) with only an automatic CLIP/VQA-based filtering step and no human verification of correctness or naturalness — this is a substantial reproducibility and validity risk, especially since the same families of generative/embedding models are reused both to construct evaluation data and to power parts of the method (e.g., VLM-approximated visual evidence patchification), raising potential for subtle self-consistent biases.

The magnitude of improvement over strong retrieval baselines (especially IKE and IKE-COT, GRACE-COT) is often modest in absolute terms on several metrics (e.g., R-Gen, Acc), while the headline claims ('greatly improves edit generalization', 'significantly improves rationale and CoE generality') are not consistently supported — IKE/GRACE without any reasoning augmentation already achieve large jumps over the unedited baseline on CoE-Gen/R-Gen in several VLM/dataset combinations, undercutting the narrative that reasoning-specific mechanisms are the primary driver.

The framing of 'editing' is blurred with retrieval-augmented prompting: ReasonEdit never updates model weights and instead prepends retrieved text to prompts, which is conceptually closer to RAG/in-context learning than to the weight-editing literature it is compared against (FT, MEND, BalancEdit); this makes some comparisons (e.g., catastrophic forgetting of weight-based editors vs. a no-weight-update retrieval system) somewhat apples-to-oranges, though the authors do include IKE/GRACE as more comparable retrieval baselines.

The topology-aware embedding selection procedure requires offline modularity calibration using external image corpora (COCO/ImageNet/Flickr30k) per VLM, adding non-trivial setup cost and raising questions about generalization to new domains (e.g., the dermatology motivating example is never actually tested, despite being the paper's running illustrative case).

No variance/statistical significance reporting across runs or seeds, and no human expert assessment of the quality of auto-generated visual evidence patches beyond an indirect CLIP similarity heuristic, limiting confidence in some of the more fine-grained claims (e.g., patch quality, generated QA correctness).

The paper is very dense with many interacting sub-components (patchification, codebook merging, modularity-based layer/weight selection, multiple novel metrics), which, combined with unverified code/data release, raises reproducibility concerns for a result set this complex.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely new and well-motivated problem setup (reasoning-enhanced VLM editing) and backs it up with two new, clearly defined evaluation metrics (Rationale Generality, Chain-of-Error Generality) that directly probe the claimed benefit of human reasoning during editing.

The topology-balanced dual embedding is a principled contribution: framing multimodal embedding selection as a graph/community-detection problem via Newman's modularity is a creative, well-justified idea, complete with scale-invariance proofs and systematic layer/weight selection procedures (Appendix A).

Extensive and fairly rigorous experimental protocol: 4 diverse VLMs, 2 rationale-annotated VQA datasets, 5 strong baselines (plus their CoT-augmented variants for fair comparison), static and sequential editing, noise-robustness analysis, and multiple ablations (embedding choice, K, retrieval threshold, key merging).

Consistent and large empirical gains over baselines across nearly all metrics and models, particularly on the newly proposed R-Gen/CoE-Gen metrics, supporting the central claim that human reasoning materially improves edit generalization.

Good attention to reproducibility: detailed algorithms (codebook construction, key merging, visual evidence patchification), hyperparameter choices justified by ablation, and demonstration that the topology-aware layer/weight selection is largely data-agnostic across three image sources.
weaknesses: Several evaluation datasets (R-Gen, CoE-Gen, image generality) are synthetically constructed using GPT-4o and diffusion models (Stable Diffusion 3, FLUX) rather than real human-collected data; this introduces potential circularity/bias (e.g., LLM-generated questions evaluated by LLM-based editors) and leaves open whether the measured gains reflect genuine reasoning generalization or artifacts of the generation pipeline.

The "human reasoning" used throughout is actually dataset-provided rationale from A-OKVQA/FVQA rather than reasoning elicited from real users interacting with the editor live; there is no user study assessing whether real human feedback would be as clean, structured, or informative as assumed (the noisy-reasoning experiment only partially addresses this via synthetic noise injection).

Correctness is determined via softmax probability over multiple-choice options rather than evaluating free-form generated answers, which may not reflect real deployment behavior of these VLMs and could inflate apparent accuracy/locality.

Key design choices such as the key-merging thresholds (90% overlap, 10% distance) and percentile-based retrieval rejection appear to be manually tuned/heuristic without strong theoretical grounding or sensitivity analysis beyond a coarse sweep.

The method requires substantial additional machinery and per-VLM calibration (Monte Carlo modularity estimation, vision layer search, weight w search, visual evidence patchification with VLM-based verification), increasing implementation complexity and computational overhead relative to simpler baselines, which is only partially quantified (e.g., embedding-selection cost is not reported alongside editing time).

Scalability of the retrieval codebook with very large numbers of edits is acknowledged as a limitation but not empirically characterized beyond ~5,000-7,000 edits, leaving open how performance/latency degrades at larger deployment scales.

The Impact Statement is minimal/boilerplate and does not meaningfully engage with potential risks of editing models based on possibly incorrect or biased user-provided reasoning (e.g., in the dermatology use case highlighted in the introduction).
